name: Marco Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an overhead crew out of the regional depot in Millbrook, the old mill town up the valley. We're in the yard by half six, I go over the job sheets with my four guys, and then it's poles and wire all day: changing out rotten poles, re-stringing a span after a truck takes one down, swapping a transformer that's cooked. I like the part where the lights come back on and some old lady waves at you from her porch. What wears me out is the paperwork and the overtime calls at two in the morning, because they always come the night after you finally got some sleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said 'my four guys'. What's your role on the crew beyond the climbing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the foreman, and I'm also the union steward for the depot, so if something's wrong, it lands on my desk, which is really the dashboard of truck forty-one. I've been at it twenty years, and I'm the one they send up when it's a tricky live job. The pay's lower than the city utilities, which everybody knows, but there's nowhere else around here to do this work since the mill shut. So I stay, and I make sure nobody on my crew gets hurt or pushed around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Every few years somebody from head office shows up with a tablet and a new system, and six months later we're back to paper and phone calls. Wires still sag, poles still rot, and somebody still has to go up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. My whole life is built on this job staying the way it is, the mortgage on Canal Street, Lena's hours at the school kitchen, the kids. If nothing radical changes, I just keep doing what I'm good at and keep fighting for a decent contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep the crew together, keep pushing at bargaining for the pay gap with the city to close, and maybe finally fix the back step on the house. I don't touch those AI programs and I wouldn't start just because they saved somebody in the office ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm, I'd say. My worries would be the same old worries, money and my back, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When you say the same old money worries, what does that look like in a normal month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We get to the end of the month with maybe a few hundred left, and that's if the car behaves. Last winter the furnace went and we put it on the card, and we're still paying that off. So 'nothing changes' isn't paradise. It just means the problems are ones I already know how to handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the AI tools you've seen at work that you'd miss if they faded away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They put an app on our phones for logging hours and it lost a week of Ray's overtime, and I spent two evenings getting it back for him. Ray's been climbing thirty years and he called that app the ghost, because things go in and never come out. If it all faded away I'd throw a little party in the yard.

S0.say: I'd tell people I told them so, because head office keeps bringing new systems that end up back on paper. Wires still sag and poles still rot, so somebody still has to go up there.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because my mortgage, my family and my whole life are built on this job staying the same. If nothing radical changes, I just keep doing what I'm good at and keep fighting for a fair contract.
S0.do: Keeps the crew together and keeps pushing at bargaining to close the pay gap with the city utilities. Carries on without AI tools, and maybe finally fixes the back step of the house.
S0.feel: Calm. His worries stay the old ones, money and his back, not robots.
S0.quote: Ray's been climbing thirty years and he called that app the ghost, because things go in and never come out.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is a foreman and union steward whose identity is tied to the crew and the depot. He's calm here, but he was quick to say that 'nothing changes' still means living close to the edge each month. His distrust of new tools comes from real experience, like the lost overtime hours, not just habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can automate the office all they like, but you can't send software up a pole in sleet. And I'd say it loud at the union meeting, because when management says 'change how you work', what they usually mean is fewer people doing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd use it to shrink crews. They already fly drones down the lines to look for damage, so the patrol guys are first. Then it's four-person crews down to three, and the fourth guy's job is to watch a screen. That's how it starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the crew-size language into the next contract, written down, no wiggle room. I'd go to the regional meetings and talk to the other stewards so we're all asking for the same thing. I wouldn't sign up for any of the training on the new tools unless the union made it part of the deal and it was paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not the end of the world, but it's that feeling when the boss calls you in and doesn't say why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the patrol guys being first. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a fella named Dev, he's fifty-five, he walks and drives the lines looking for cracked insulators and leaning poles. He's got a bad knee, so patrol is what keeps him working until his pension. If a drone does his job, where does he go, up a pole at fifty-five with that knee? That's the guy I'd lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say the new tools could make the job safer. How do you see that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure, if a machine can tell me a line's still live before I touch it, I'll take it. But I've seen 'safety' used as the reason to cut a man from a crew, and a three-person crew in a storm is not safer, I don't care what the spreadsheet says. If they want safety, they can give us the fourth guy and the gadget.

S1.say: I'd say they can automate the office, but you can't send software up a pole in sleet. I'd also say at the union meeting that 'change how you work' usually means fewer people doing more.
S1.think: I think they'd use the change to shrink crews, starting with the line patrol jobs that drones can do. Four-person crews would become three, and the fourth person would end up watching a screen.
S1.do: Pushes to get crew-size rules written into the next union contract and coordinates with stewards from other depots. Refuses training on new tools unless the union makes it paid and part of the deal.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like being called into the boss's office without a reason. It isn't a disaster, but it nags.
S1.quote: A three-person crew in a storm is not safer, I don't care what the spreadsheet says.
S1.fieldNote: His worry here is more for others than himself, especially Dev, the older patrol worker with a bad knee. He sees the union contract as his main tool and reads every new device as a staffing question. He accepts safety gadgets in principle but distrusts how management would use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal, and that the people who built this should be made to pay for the mess. I'd be on every picket line and every bus to the capital. And I'd tell my crew straight that nobody's coming to save us unless we make noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I don't think I'd come through it. We've got less than a month of money saved. If I lose the job in 2028, the bank has the house by the end of the year, and there's no other line work around here, there's nothing around here at all since the mill. I don't know computers, I've never even used one of those chat programs. Two years is nothing. Theo would still be in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd stop every spend that isn't food, fuel or the mortgage: no hockey for Theo, no new boots. I'd go to the union and push for a fight over severance and a hold on layoffs, and I'd push the government for some kind of income for people like us, because it's the only thing that would work in two years. And I'd probably call my brother in the city and ask, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I'd be scared out of my mind and trying not to show it at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say nothing, and she'd know anyway, because I go quiet. Then after the kids were in bed I'd sit at the kitchen table with the bills spread out, and she'd sit across from me. I think I'd say, 'I'm sorry, I don't know how to fix this one.' I've never said that to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody's coming to save you, but you'd also push the government for an income. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. What I mean is nobody's coming unless we force them. A government doesn't hand anything out because it's kind, it does it because ten thousand people are outside with signs. So the noise is the plan. The income is what the noise is for.

S2.say: I'd call it a scandal and say the people who built it should pay for the mess. I'd be on every picket line and tell my crew that nobody saves us unless we make noise.
S2.think: I don't think we'd come through it, with less than a month saved and no other line work in the valley. Two years is nothing, and I've never even used a chat program, so I'd have nowhere to go.
S2.do: Cuts everything except food, fuel and the mortgage, starting with his son's hockey. Pushes the union to fight for severance and a hold on layoffs, campaigns for a government income, and asks his brother for help for the first time.
S2.feel: Terrified, as if the floor has gone, while trying to hide it at the dinner table.
S2.quote: I think I'd say, 'I'm sorry, I don't know how to fix this one.' I've never said that to her.
S2.fieldNote: This is where his steadiness breaks. With thin savings, no local alternatives and no comfort with technology, two years leaves him with no plan except collective pressure. The moment of admitting defeat to his partner was the most honest part of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, only louder and earlier: we've got five years, so start writing the rules now. Who gets paid when the robot climbs the pole? That's the question I'd be asking anybody who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of room, but not much. I'd be forty-eight. I'm still no good with computers and I'm not going to become a programmer. What it really gives me is time to organize, and time to get the debt down so we're not one paycheck from losing the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start paying off the card and the furnace loan right away, and put whatever overtime I get into a savings account instead of the car. I'd get the stewards from all the depots together the first year and draft what we want: retraining paid by the company, a bridge income, early pension for guys like Dev. And I'd vote for whoever puts that in writing, and knock on doors for them if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but scared with something to do. That's different from the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd try to learn in those five years, even if it's not programming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena keeps telling me to learn how to use the phone stuff properly, and maybe I would, enough to read the contracts and keep up. But I'm not going to pretend I'd become a robot technician. My hands know poles and wire. What I'd learn is how to run a campaign, because that's what I'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop pretending. Mia wants to do dance, and we'd probably say not this year. Theo would be leaving school right about when it lands, and I'd sit him down and tell him not to follow me up the pole, which breaks my heart, because I always thought he would. We'd talk about money at the table instead of after they're in bed.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so we should start writing the rules now. I'd keep asking who gets paid when the robot climbs the pole.
S3.think: Five years gives me a little room, but I'd be forty-eight and I won't become a programmer. Mostly it gives me time to organize and to get the debt down so we aren't one paycheck from losing the house.
S3.do: Pays down the credit card and furnace loan and puts overtime into savings instead of the car. Brings stewards from all depots together in the first year to draft demands for paid retraining, a bridge income and early pensions, and votes and campaigns for whoever backs them.
S3.feel: Scared, but with something to do, which feels different from the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Who gets paid when the robot climbs the pole? That's the question I'd be asking anybody who'd listen.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time moves him from despair into organizing and paying down debt, but he is still losing sleep because he can't see a personal way out. Telling his son not to follow him into the trade was a painful turning point. He frames learning as learning to campaign, not learning technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say we've got no excuse. If the government and the company can't build a fair way through this with a decade's warning, then they never meant to. I'd make sure every member of my local knew the date and what we were asking for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd be fifty-three when it lands. The kids would be grown or nearly. If I can get the mortgage down and the union wins an early pension at fifty-five or so, I might squeak through. It's still the end of the job I love, but it might not be the end of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a real savings cushion over the first few years, even if it's small, and stop all extra spending on the truck. I'd make the union's main fight for the next ten years a bridge to pension for anyone over fifty. And I'd help the young guys on my crew get out early, into whatever's still standing, because they've got time I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. Like before a big storm, when you know it's coming and you get the trucks ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help the young guys get out early. What would you actually tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a kid, Jordan, twenty-four, best climber I've seen in years. I'd tell him: you're good, but don't bet your life on this. Use the next five years to get papers in something, and I'd sign whatever reference he needs. It'd hurt, because I'd be training somebody to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared to the two-year picture, what does the extra time change most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year one I'm a guy with no options and no money. In this one I've got time to save, time for the kids to grow up, and time for the union to win something. Same robots at the end, but I'm not the one who gets crushed by them. That's the whole difference, the time.

S4.say: With ten years of warning, I'd say there's no excuse for not building a fair way through it. I'd make sure every member of my local knew the date and what we were asking for.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three when it lands, with the kids grown. If I get the mortgage down and the union wins an early pension, I might squeak through, even though it's still the end of the job I love.
S4.do: Builds a small savings cushion over the first few years and stops extra spending on the truck. Makes a bridge to pension for workers over fifty the union's main fight, and helps younger crew members get qualifications to leave early.
S4.feel: Worried but steady, like getting the trucks ready before a storm he knows is coming.
S4.quote: Same robots at the end, but I'm not the one who gets crushed by them. That's the whole difference, the time.
S4.fieldNote: The decade turns the threat into a pension and timing problem he can work on. His thinking shifts to the younger crew, and he's willing to help Jordan leave even though it hurts. He still puts his hope in collective bargaining rather than his own reinvention.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. With thin savings and nothing else in this valley, two years means we lose the house. What would help is a bridge income that kicks in when the job goes, paid for by whoever's making the money from the robots, and an early pension for anyone over fifty who's given their body to this work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the body. People think this job is just wire, but my shoulders are shot and I'm forty-three. Half of why I'd fight for an early pension is that I can't climb at sixty anyway. Robots or no robots, guys like me are running on borrowed knees.

headlineQuote: Robots or no robots, guys like me are running on borrowed knees.
portrait: Marco Dubois is a 43-year-old overhead line foreman and union steward at a regional depot in a former mill town, with a partner who cooks in a school kitchen, two kids and a mortgage on a house they can barely carry. He's among the best climbers in the region but earns less than city lineworkers and has almost no savings. He distrusts new technology and never uses AI tools, and his answer to every threat is the union. He's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy about crew cuts in a steady change, but the two-year AGI picture leaves him panicked, while five and ten years turn his fear into organizing, paying down debt and pushing for an early pension.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because with less than a month saved and no other work in the valley, two years would cost his family the house.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge income when the job goes, paid for by those profiting from the robots, and an early pension for workers over fifty who've worn out their bodies on the job.
